summary: This note traces the history of waste-to-energy (WtE) technologies from late 19th-century incinerators to modern bioconversion, thermal and community-based plants. It highlights regulatory milestones, key researchers and landmark facilities, including plasma gasification, Amager Bakke and hydrothermal carbonization. It concludes that WtE is becoming a core part of the circular economy, with waste serving as a starting point for energy and materials.
one_line: A historical overview of waste-to-energy technology, from early incinerators to gasification, bioconversion, hydrothermal carbonization and circular-economy integration.
key_facts: The first waste incinerators were developed in the late 19th century to reduce municipal waste volume.

The oil crises of the 1970s made the world start treating waste as a potential energy source; engineers Edward Hargrove and Marjorie Jones experimented with energy recovery in response to oil shortages.
On October 16, 1985, the US Environmental Protection Agency enacted stringent emissions standards, driving advanced combustion techniques that minimized toxic emissions and improved energy retrieval.
Dr. Anita Wolfe helped create processes to filter and capture pollutants, making energy-from-waste facilities competitive with conventional power plants.
Gasification and pyrolysis were introduced in the early 1990s; gasification uses a restricted oxygen environment to convert organic materials into syngas with fewer harmful emissions.
On September 4, 1994, a team led by Dr. Ian Richardson unveiled a plasma gasification facility in Yorkshire, England, which used high temperatures to ionize waste.
Paul Connett's 'The Zero Waste Solution', released September 12, 2002, urged integrating WtE into a comprehensive waste strategy that minimized landfill use.
Copenhagen's Amager Bakke, unveiled on September 8, 2010, converts trash to energy and has a ski slope on its roof.

On September 15, 2019, Dr. Luisa Hernandez's team in Barcelona, Spain, implemented a bio-digestion process that let biogas plants handle a broader range of organic wastes, such as food scraps and agricultural residue.
On September 18, 2023, a European consortium led by Dr. Emma Berglund introduced a commercial-scale hydrothermal carbonization plant in Sweden that turns wet organic waste into bio-coal.
On September 27, 2021, Albuquerque, New Mexico's city council and GreenFuture Technologies launched a network of small-scale, community-oriented WtE plants providing local energy and jobs.
WtE plants increasingly function as production units within a broader materials management system tied to the circular economy.
